items.title: L6: Cutting a draft down: hidden verbs and padding
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design: planning, writing and managing content
items.body:
A common cause of heavy writing is the hidden verb, where an action is buried in a noun. 'We will make a decision' hides the verb 'decide'. 'Give consideration to' means 'consider', 'carry out an investigation into' means 'investigate' and 'is in receipt of' means 'has' or 'gets'. Turning the noun back into a verb usually shortens the sentence and makes it easier to read.

Padding is the second cause. Throat-clearing openings such as 'I am writing to let you know that' delay the point, and phrases such as 'please note that' rarely add anything. Replace 'in the event that' with 'if', 'with regard to' with 'about' and 'in order to' with 'to'. Cut intensifiers such as 'very' and 'really'.

Stacked nouns, such as 'claim processing delay resolution timetable', force the reader to unpick the meaning. Break them up: 'when we will fix the delay in processing your claim'. Avoid double negatives such as 'not unless' or 'not uncommon' and say the positive instead.

The passive voice is not banned. It is fine when the person doing the action is unknown or unimportant, for example 'Your payment has been sent'. It is a problem when it hides who must act: 'Evidence must be provided' does not say who provides it.

When editing, keep the meaning and every fact, cut the words that do no work, and read the result aloud. Do not remove legal wording that has to be accurate, but explain it in plain English next to it. Always check that dates, amounts and names survive the edit unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of 'We will give consideration to your appeal and make a decision by 12 June' removes the hidden verbs?

options.text: We will give your appeal careful consideration and decide by 12 June.
We will consider your appeal and decide by 12 June.
We will make a decision on your appeal after consideration by 12 June.
Your appeal will be considered and a decision will be made by 12 June.

questions.hint: Replacing 'give consideration to' and 'make a decision' with 'consider' and 'decide' turns the buried nouns back into verbs.

questions.prompt: A draft opens: 'I am writing to let you know that we have now received your application.' What is the best edit?

options.text: We have received your application.
We would like to inform you that your application has been received by us.
Please note that we have now received your application.
I am writing to confirm that your application has now been received.

questions.hint: The throat-clearing opening delays the point, so the fact should come straight away.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is the best plain replacement for 'in the event that you are unable to attend'?

options.text: in case you are not able to attend
should you be unable to attend
where attendance is not possible for you
if you cannot attend

questions.hint: 'In the event that' is padding for 'if', and 'cannot' is shorter than 'are unable to'.

questions.prompt: 'Claim processing delay resolution timetable' is a stack of nouns. Which rewrite untangles it best?

options.text: the timetable for the resolution of claim processing delays
the processing timetable for resolving claim delays
when we will fix the delay in processing your claim
claim delay resolution: processing timetable

questions.hint: Breaking a noun stack into a clause with a verb tells the reader who does what.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the passive voice in a way that is acceptable?

options.text: Your payment has been sent to your bank.
Your change of address must be reported to the office.
The form should be completed and returned within 14 days.
Evidence of your income must be provided before we can pay.

questions.hint: The passive is fine when the actor is unimportant, but the other options hide who must act.

questions.prompt: Why is 'Evidence must be provided by 5 May' a weak sentence for a customer letter?

options.text: It uses a word that is too long for the reader
It gives a date in a style the GOV.UK guide does not allow
It puts the deadline before the action
It does not say who must provide the evidence

questions.hint: Hiding the actor in the passive leaves the reader unsure whether they or someone else must act.

questions.prompt: Which edit follows the advice on double negatives?

options.text: Changing 'We cannot pay if you do not send proof' to 'We are unable to pay if you do not send proof'
Changing 'You will not receive payment unless you reply' to 'You will not get payment unless you reply'
Changing 'It is not uncommon for claims to be delayed' to 'It is not unusual for claims to be delayed'
Changing 'It is not uncommon for claims to be delayed' to 'Claims are often delayed'

questions.hint: Saying the positive directly removes the need for the reader to cancel out two negatives.

questions.prompt: You are editing a paragraph that quotes a legal test word for word. What is the right approach?

options.text: Shorten the legal test by cutting any words you think are padding
Remove the test and refer the reader to the legislation instead
Keep the exact legal wording and add a plain English explanation next to it
Rewrite the legal test completely in your own plain words and delete the original

questions.hint: Legal wording may need to stay accurate, so explain it alongside rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: After cutting a draft from 400 to 250 words, what check matters most before sending?

options.text: That every sentence now starts with the word 'we'
That the new draft has at least one sentence in the passive voice
That every date, amount and name is still correct and the meaning has not changed
That the opening paragraph is longer than the closing paragraph

questions.hint: Editing must never change facts, so figures and meaning are the first thing to check.

items.title: L6: GOV.UK style: bullets, links and emphasis
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide: lists, links, bold, abbreviations and Latin
items.body:
The GOV.UK style guide sets out detailed rules that most government writers follow. For bullet lists, use a lead-in line that ends with a colon, start each bullet with a lower-case letter and do not put a full stop at the end of a bullet. Where the bullets are alternatives, the lead-in often makes this clear, for example 'You can apply if you:'. Do not use semicolons to separate bullets. Use a numbered list only when the order matters, such as steps.

Link text should make sense on its own and describe where the link goes, for example 'check how to renew your passport'. Do not use 'click here' or 'read more', because screen reader users often move between links and hear them out of context. Do not use a bare web address as link text in running copy, and do not link the same page repeatedly in one paragraph.

Do not use bold for emphasis in running text, and avoid italics and underlining, because underlined text looks like a link. Use headings to give structure instead. Headings use sentence case, with a capital only for the first word and proper nouns, and do not end in a full stop.

Do not use Latin abbreviations such as 'e.g.', 'i.e.' and 'etc'. Write 'for example', 'that is' and 'and so on'. Spell out an abbreviation the first time it is used, unless it is very well known, and avoid '&' in running text.

Use 'must' for a legal requirement or an obligation, and 'should' for a recommendation. Using 'must' makes clear that there is no choice.

questions.prompt: Which bullet list follows GOV.UK style?

options.text:
You can apply if you
- are 18 or over.
- live in England.
- have a valid passport.

You can apply if you:
- are 18 or over
- live in England
- have a valid passport

You can apply if you:
1) are 18 or over
2) live in England
3) have a valid passport

questions.hint: Use a colon lead-in, lower-case starts and no full stops or semicolons on bullets.

questions.prompt: When should a numbered list be used instead of bullets?

options.text: When the list has more than five items
When each item is a full sentence
When the items are all of equal importance
When the items are steps that must be done in order

questions.hint: Numbers signal sequence, so use them only where order matters.

questions.prompt: Which link text best follows the guidance?

options.text: check how to renew your passport
click here to renew your passport
https://www.gov.uk/renew-adult-passport
read more

questions.hint: Link text should describe the destination and make sense when read out of context.

questions.prompt: Why is 'click here' poor link text?

options.text: It is a phrase the GOV.UK guide treats as Latin
It is longer than a plain description would be
Screen reader users often hear links listed out of context, so it tells them nothing
It only works on a mouse and not on a touch screen

questions.hint: Assistive technology can list all links on a page, so each must be meaningful by itself.

questions.prompt: Why does GOV.UK style advise against underlining text for emphasis?

options.text: Underlining is only allowed in headings
Underlined text looks like a link
Underlined words are skipped by screen readers
Underlining prints badly on most office printers

questions.hint: Readers expect underlined text to be clickable, so it confuses.

questions.prompt: Which heading follows GOV.UK style?

options.text: Who Can Apply For This Help.
Who Is Eligible To Apply
Who can apply for this help
WHO CAN APPLY FOR THIS HELP:

questions.hint: Headings use sentence case and have no full stop.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct under GOV.UK style?

options.text: Bring photo ID, e.g. a passport or driving licence.
Bring photo ID (i.e. a passport or driving licence).
Bring photo ID, for example a passport or driving licence.
Bring photo ID such as a passport, driving licence, etc.

questions.hint: Latin abbreviations are avoided in favour of 'for example' and 'that is'.

questions.prompt: A letter says: 'Employers should pay the minimum wage', where the law requires it. Which change is best?

options.text: Leave it, as 'should' and 'must' mean the same
Change 'should' to 'are encouraged to'
Change 'should' to 'ought to'
Change 'should' to 'must'

questions.hint: Use 'must' for obligations, so the reader knows there is no choice.

questions.prompt: When may you use an abbreviation such as 'HMRC' in a paragraph without spelling it out?

options.text: Only in headings and subject lines
Never rely on it: spell out the full name the first time unless the abbreviation is very well known
Always, because organisations choose their own abbreviations
Only when the document is longer than a page

questions.hint: Spell out on first use so every reader knows what the short form stands for.

items.title: L6: Emails: forwarding, chains and Bcc
items.source: Civil Service Code; ICO guidance on sending personal data by email; GOV.UK guidance on writing for users
items.body:
Many email mistakes in government come from chains and recipient fields. Before you forward a long chain, scroll to the bottom. Earlier messages may contain personal data, commercial details or comments never meant for the new recipient. Either delete the parts the new reader should not see or write a fresh summary instead. When you forward, add a line at the top saying why you are sending it and what you want the reader to do.

Use Bcc (blind carbon copy) when you send one message to many members of the public who do not know each other. If you put them all in To or Cc, each person can see everyone's email address, and that is a personal data breach. A better option for large mailings is a mail-merge or a bulk-email service that sends each person a separate message.

Reply All sends your answer to everyone on the original message. Use it only when everyone needs the reply. A one-word 'thanks' to 200 people wastes their time.

Change the subject line when the topic of a chain changes, because people search and sort by subject. Keep one subject for one issue. Use your out-of-office message to say when you are away and who to contact, but do not give reasons such as an illness or details of your location.

Remember that emails are records. They may be disclosed under the Freedom of Information Act or in response to a subject access request, so write nothing you would not be happy to see read out. Avoid capital letters for emphasis, which can read as shouting.

questions.prompt: You are asked to forward a long chain to an external supplier. What should you do first?

options.text: Forward it as an attachment so the text cannot be searched
Read the whole chain and remove or summarise any content the supplier should not see
Add the supplier to Bcc so that earlier senders cannot see them
Check that the supplier's address is in the To field and send it

questions.hint: Earlier messages in a chain may hold personal or sensitive content that the new recipient should not receive.

questions.prompt: You send an update to 80 members of the public who do not know each other. How should you address it?

options.text: Put the recipients in Bcc, or use a mail-merge so each gets their own message
Put all of them in Cc so that everyone can see who else was told
Put the first ten in To and the rest in Bcc to save time
Put them in To and ask them not to reply to all

questions.hint: Showing everyone's address to the group is a personal data breach.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Reply All is correct?

options.text: It sends the reply to everyone in your department
It sends your reply only to the person who wrote the last message
It sends your reply to everyone including those in Bcc
It sends your reply to everyone on the original message, including those in To and Cc

questions.hint: Reply All covers To and Cc recipients of the message, not hidden Bcc readers.

questions.prompt: A chain started as a question about room bookings but now discusses a staff rota. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the original subject so the history stays together
Delete the subject line so it cannot mislead anyone
Start a new message or change the subject line to match the new topic
Add the word URGENT to the existing subject

questions.hint: An accurate subject line helps people find and prioritise messages.

questions.prompt: Which out-of-office message is the best?

options.text: I am away. Your email has not been read and will be deleted.
I am on holiday in Spain until 9 June with no access to email. Contact my manager on her mobile.
I am out of the office until Monday 9 June. For urgent queries contact the team inbox at the address below.
I am off sick until further notice and will reply when I am back at my desk.

questions.hint: State dates and an alternative contact without giving private reasons or locations.

questions.prompt: Why should you write each email on the basis that it could be disclosed?

options.text: Emails can be released under FOI or in a subject access request
Emails are automatically published on GOV.UK after a year
Only emails marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE can be disclosed
Disclosure applies only to letters, not emails

questions.hint: Email is held information and may have to be released if requested lawfully.

questions.prompt: Which is the best opening line when forwarding a message to a colleague?

options.text: FYI
Please can you reply to this customer by Friday? Her complaint is below.
See below.
Forwarded for your information and action as appropriate.

questions.hint: A forwarded email should say why you are sending it and what you want done by when.

questions.prompt: You sent an email with a customer's name and claim number to the wrong external address. What is the right first step?

options.text: Send a second email asking the recipient to delete the first
Wait to see whether the recipient replies before reporting
Tell your manager or data protection contact straight away and follow the reporting process
Try to recall the email and say nothing if the recall works

questions.hint: Report a possible breach promptly so it can be assessed within time limits.

questions.prompt: Why is writing in capital letters throughout an email unwise?

options.text: It is only allowed in the subject line
It makes the email larger and more likely to be blocked as spam
It can come across as shouting and is harder to read
It breaks the GOV.UK rule on bold text

questions.hint: Plain sentence case reads more calmly and is easier to scan.

items.title: L6: Letters: giving reasons, review rights and accessible formats
items.source: Equality Act 2010; GOV.UK Service Manual; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman guidance on good administration
items.body:
A decision letter should put the decision first, then the reasons, then what the person can do next. A customer who gets a refusal needs to know three things: what was decided, why it was decided, and how to challenge it. Give the reasons in specific terms ('your income was above the limit of the benefit') rather than vague ones ('you do not meet the criteria'). Quote the law only where it helps the reader, and explain it.

Say clearly how to ask for a review or appeal, who to contact and the deadline. A deadline should be a date. Be careful with phrases such as 'within one month': say whether the month runs from the date of the letter or the date it was received, and give the actual last date where possible.

Under the Equality Act 2010, public bodies must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, and the Public Sector Equality Duty requires them to think about the needs of people with protected characteristics. In practice, offer information in other formats, such as large print, Braille, audio, Easy Read or British Sign Language, and say how to ask for them. Customers should not have to ask twice. If a person tells you of a need, record it so the next letter arrives in the right format.

Offer a plain language route to complain. If the complaint is not resolved by the department, the person can usually ask their MP to refer it to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. Give a name or a team and a contact route so the customer knows who to contact, not just a generic inbox.

questions.prompt: In what order should a decision letter normally present its content?

options.text: An apology, the law, then the decision
The decision, the reasons, then what the person can do next
The reasons, the decision, then an apology
Background, the law, the decision, then next steps

questions.hint: People want the outcome first, followed by why and what they can do about it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the reason for refusal most helpfully?

options.text: We cannot pay because your income of £28,000 is above the limit of £25,000.
We cannot pay because you do not meet the criteria.
Your claim is refused under the relevant regulations.
After careful consideration we have decided not to award payment.

questions.hint: A specific reason lets the customer see whether the decision is right and decide whether to challenge it.

questions.prompt: A letter says 'You must ask for a review within one month'. What is the main weakness?

options.text: It is too short to count as a review right
It does not say when the month starts or give the actual last date
It does not say who made the decision
It uses a time period rather than a word

questions.hint: Unclear starting points cause people to miss deadlines, so state the date.

questions.prompt: A customer tells you they are blind and cannot read standard print. What does the Equality Act 2010 expect a public body to do?

options.text: Ask for medical evidence before changing the format of any letter
Send standard letters and read them out on the telephone only on request
Offer the format only if the customer asks again in writing
Make a reasonable adjustment such as providing information in Braille, audio or large print

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are a duty, and the department should not make the customer jump through hoops.

questions.prompt: After a customer asks for Easy Read letters, what should you do to make sure later letters arrive in that format?

options.text: Record the need on the case or customer record so it applies to all future letters
Put a flag on the customer's file only if they ask a second time
Make a note in your own diary for future letters
Tell the customer to ask each time they receive a letter

questions.hint: A recorded need helps every colleague, so customers do not have to repeat requests.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to describe a deadline for a challenge in a letter dated 5 March?

options.text: Say 'promptly, so that we can progress your case'.
Say 'in 30 days' without a start point.
Say 'within a reasonable time of this letter'.
Give the last date, for example: 'Contact us by 4 April 2025.'

questions.hint: A clear date is easier to act on than a period.

questions.prompt: A customer says they are unhappy with the department's final complaint response. What can they usually do next?

options.text: Appeal directly to the Cabinet Office complaints team
Send the complaint to the National Archives
Ask their MP to refer the complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Ask the Information Commissioner to review the complaint about service

questions.hint: The Ombudsman considers unresolved complaints about government services, normally via an MP referral.

questions.prompt: Why should a letter name a team or contact route instead of just 'the department'?

options.text: Because it makes the letter look longer and more formal
Because letters with team names are exempt from the Equality Act
Because naming a team removes the need for an apology
So the customer knows who to contact and how, and the query reaches the right place

questions.hint: A clear contact route reduces repeat contact and customer frustration.

questions.prompt: Which format is NOT normally offered as an accessible alternative to a standard printed letter?

options.text: A longer letter with more legal references
Large print
Braille
Easy Read

questions.hint: Accessible formats change how information is delivered; adding legal references would make it harder to read.

items.title: L6: Spreadsheets: nested IF, AND and OR
items.source: Microsoft Support: IF, nested IF, AND and OR functions; GOV.UK guidance on using spreadsheets
items.body:
The IF function tests a condition and returns one result if it is true and another if it is false: =IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). If you leave out the third argument and the test is false, Excel returns FALSE. If you write a test but the cell is empty, Excel treats the empty cell as zero in a number test.

To choose between more than two results, nest IFs: put another IF in the value_if_false position. A grade formula might be =IF(B2>=70,"Distinction",IF(B2>=50,"Merit",IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail"))). Excel works from left to right and stops at the first test that is true, so the order matters. If you tested B2>=40 first, a score of 65 would return "Pass" and never reach the later tests. With three results you need two IFs, with four results you need three IFs, and so on. Each IF needs its own closing bracket.

AND returns TRUE only if every condition is true. OR returns TRUE if at least one condition is true. They are normally used inside IF: =IF(AND(A2>=18,B2="Yes"),"Eligible","Not eligible"). Text in a formula must be inside double quotation marks. Text comparisons are not case sensitive, so "yes" equals "Yes".

Percentages and numbers can be compared directly. Do not put quotation marks around a number in a test, because "50" is text and will not compare as a number.

A long nested IF is hard to check. Where there are many bands, a lookup table with VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP is usually easier to maintain.

questions.prompt: Using =IF(B2>=70,"Distinction",IF(B2>=50,"Merit",IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail"))), what is returned when B2 holds 65?

options.text: Merit
Fail
Pass
Distinction

questions.hint: 65 fails the first test (70) but passes the second (50), so the result is Merit.

questions.prompt: If scores are whole numbers, what is the lowest score that returns "Pass" from that grade formula?
questions.hint: The last test is B2>=40, so 40 itself qualifies.

questions.prompt: Why does each test in the grade formula use >= rather than >?

options.text: So that the formula can be copied down without changing
So that a score exactly on a threshold gets the higher result
So that Excel treats the score as text
So that blank cells return Fail

questions.hint: With > a score of exactly 70 would miss Distinction.

questions.prompt: Someone writes =IF(B2>=40,"Pass",IF(B2>=50,"Merit",IF(B2>=70,"Distinction","Fail"))). What does it return for 65?

options.text: Pass
Merit
Fail
Distinction

questions.hint: The first true test wins, and 65 is at least 40, so the later tests are never reached.

questions.prompt: How many IF functions are needed to return one of five different results from a single value?

options.text: Five
Two
Four
Three

questions.hint: Each IF splits off one outcome, so n results need n minus 1 IFs.

questions.prompt: What does =IF(A1>5,"High") display when A1 holds 3?

options.text: An empty cell
Low
#VALUE!
FALSE

questions.hint: If the false result is omitted, Excel returns the logical value FALSE.

questions.prompt: Cell A2 holds 20 and B2 holds "yes". What does =IF(AND(A2>=18,B2="Yes"),"Eligible","Not eligible") return?

options.text: Eligible
Not eligible
FALSE
#NAME?

questions.hint: Both conditions are true, and text comparisons ignore case so "yes" equals "Yes".

questions.prompt: A2 holds 16 and B2 holds "Yes". What does =IF(OR(A2>=18,B2="Yes"),"Pass","Fail") return?

options.text: FALSE
Fail
#N/A
Pass

questions.hint: OR needs only one true condition, and B2="Yes" is true.

questions.prompt: A2 is blank. What does =IF(A2>=50,"Pass","Fail") return?

options.text: Fail
An empty cell
Pass
#VALUE!

questions.hint: A blank cell counts as zero in a numeric comparison, so the test is false.

questions.prompt: Which version of the test is wrong because the number is treated as text?

options.text: =IF(A2>=25*2,"Pass","Fail")
=IF(A2>="50","Pass","Fail")
=IF(A2>=B1,"Pass","Fail")
=IF(A2>=50,"Pass","Fail")

questions.hint: Quotation marks around a number turn it into text, which does not compare as a number.

items.title: L6: Spreadsheets: VLOOKUP exact and approximate matches
items.source: Microsoft Support: VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP functions
items.body:
VLOOKUP has four arguments: =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]). The lookup value is searched for in the first column of the table, and the function returns the value from the column number you give, counting from the left, where the first column is 1.

The last argument matters. FALSE (or 0) asks for an exact match. If the value is not found, you get #N/A. TRUE (or 1) asks for an approximate match: Excel finds the largest value that is less than or equal to the lookup value. For this to work, the first column must be sorted in ascending order. If you leave out the fourth argument, Excel assumes TRUE, which is a common cause of wrong answers when looking up IDs.

A typical use of approximate match is a banding table. Suppose F2:G4 holds 0 with 0%, 1000 with 2%, and 5000 with 5%. Then =VLOOKUP(2500,F2:G4,2,TRUE) returns 2%, because 1000 is the largest threshold not above 2500. A value of 4999 returns 2% and 5000 returns 5%. A value below the first threshold, such as -5, returns #N/A.

If the column number is larger than the number of columns in the table, VLOOKUP returns #REF!. If the column number is less than 1, it returns #VALUE!. VLOOKUP can only look to the right of the lookup column. When you need to look left, use XLOOKUP or INDEX with MATCH.

XLOOKUP takes =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found]). It defaults to an exact match, and the fourth argument lets you show your own message instead of #N/A.

questions.prompt: A banding table in F2:G4 has 0 with 0%, 1000 with 2% and 5000 with 5%. What does =VLOOKUP(2500,F2:G4,2,TRUE) return?

options.text: #N/A

questions.hint: Approximate match returns the largest threshold not above 2500, which is 1000.

questions.prompt: Which lookup value is the lowest that returns 5% from that banding table with approximate match?
questions.hint: The 5000 row applies from 5000 upwards, and the exact threshold is included.

questions.prompt: Why must the first column of a banding table be sorted ascending for approximate match?

options.text: Sorted data is needed so that blank cells return zero
Sorting lets the column_index number be larger than the table width
Excel searches for the largest value not above the lookup value, and unsorted data can give wrong answers
Excel needs sorted data before it can find any exact match

questions.hint: Approximate match relies on the order of the first column.

questions.prompt: A negative lookup value of -5 is used against the banding table with TRUE. What is returned?

options.text: #VALUE!
#N/A
#REF!

questions.hint: A value below the smallest entry in the first column cannot be matched.

questions.prompt: You look up staff ID 20417 in a table of IDs, but the formula omits the last argument and returns the wrong person. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The missing fourth argument defaults to approximate match
The IDs are in the wrong colour format
The table has no column headings
The formula needs a dollar sign before the ID

questions.hint: Leaving out range_lookup means TRUE, so Excel returns the nearest lower ID instead of an exact one.

questions.prompt: A VLOOKUP uses a table_array of A2:C20 and a col_index_num of 4. What is returned?

options.text: #N/A
#VALUE!
#REF!
The last column's value

questions.hint: The table has only three columns, so column 4 does not exist.

questions.prompt: What does a col_index_num of 0 cause in VLOOKUP?

options.text: #N/A
The lookup column's value
#VALUE!
#REF!

questions.hint: The column index must be 1 or higher, so Excel returns a #VALUE! error.

questions.prompt: You need to return the department name that sits to the left of the employee ID column. Which approach works?

options.text: =XLOOKUP(E2,C:C,A:A)
=VLOOKUP(E2,A:C,-2,FALSE)
=VLOOKUP(E2,A:C,1,FALSE)
=VLOOKUP(E2,C:A,1,FALSE)

questions.hint: VLOOKUP only looks right of the lookup column, whereas XLOOKUP can return from any column.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the fourth argument in =XLOOKUP(A2,B:B,C:C,"Not found")?

options.text: It stops the formula returning errors in other cells
It shows a custom message instead of #N/A if there is no match
It sorts the lookup column
It sets the match to approximate

questions.hint: The if_not_found argument replaces the default #N/A.

items.title: L6: Spreadsheets: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS with several conditions
items.source: Microsoft Support: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS functions
items.body:
SUMIFS adds up values that meet several conditions. Its order of arguments differs from SUMIF: the range to add comes first. The form is =SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...). COUNTIFS has no sum range and has pairs of range and criteria: =COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...). All conditions must be true for a row to count (AND logic). All ranges must be the same size.

Criteria can be text, numbers or expressions in quotation marks. Examples: "North" matches the text, ">100" means above 100, ">=100" means 100 or more, "<>North" means anything except North and "N*" matches any text starting with N. To use a value held in a cell, join the operator and the cell with an ampersand: ">="&C1.

Use this small table. Team, region, cases handled: A North 120; B South 90; C North 150; D East 60; E South 110; F North 80; G East 140; H South 70.

Then =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"North",C2:C9,">100") adds only North rows with more than 100 cases, which are A (120) and C (150), giving 270. =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"South",C2:C9,"<100") counts South rows below 100 (B and H), which is 2.

To get an average for a group, divide a conditional sum by a conditional count, or use AVERAGEIFS. To count rows that match one condition OR another, add two COUNTIFS together or use SUM with an array of criteria, because COUNTIFS on its own uses AND.

questions.prompt: The table has North rows of 120, 150 and 80 cases. What does =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"North",C2:C9,">100") return?
questions.hint: Only the North rows above 100 count: 120 plus 150.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"South",C2:C9,"<100") return, given South rows of 90, 110 and 70?
questions.hint: Only the South rows of 90 and 70 are below 100.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"<>North") return?
questions.hint: It adds every row whose region is not North: 90+60+110+140+70.

questions.prompt: Cell E1 holds 100. Which formula counts the rows with 100 or more cases?

options.text: =COUNTIFS(C2:C9,">=",E1)
=COUNTIFS(C2:C9,>=E1)
=COUNTIFS(C2:C9,">="&E1)
=COUNTIFS(C2:C9,">=E1")

questions.hint: To use a cell value with an operator, join them with an ampersand outside the quotation marks.

questions.prompt: What number does =COUNTIFS(C2:C9,">="&E1) return when E1 holds 100?
questions.hint: The rows with 100 or more are 120, 150, 110 and 140.

questions.prompt: What is the average number of cases for North, given the sum of 350 over three rows?

options.text: 116.7, from =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"North")/COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"North")
175, from dividing the sum by two
350, from =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"North")
120, from taking the first North row

questions.hint: 350 divided by 3 is 116.67 to two decimal places, or 116.7 to one.

questions.prompt: A colleague writes =SUMIFS(B2:B9,"North",C2:C9) to add the case counts. What is wrong?

options.text: The formula needs a final TRUE argument
Both ranges must be in the same column
SUMIFS cannot use text criteria
The sum range must come first, then each criteria range followed by its criterion

questions.hint: SUMIFS expects sum_range then range-criterion pairs, unlike SUMIF.

questions.prompt: Which criteria matches every region whose name starts with N?
questions.hint: An asterisk is the wildcard for any number of characters.

questions.prompt: How should you count rows where the region is South OR East?

options.text: Use =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"South"&"East")
Use =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"South",B2:B9,"East")
Use one COUNTIFS with both regions in the same criteria range
Add =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"South") and =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"East")

questions.hint: COUNTIFS uses AND logic, so separate counts must be added together for OR.

items.title: L6: Spreadsheets: text functions for tidying references
items.source: Microsoft Support: LEFT, MID, RIGHT, LEN, FIND, TRIM, PROPER and TEXT functions
items.body:
Text functions help to split, clean and rebuild data such as case references and names. LEFT(text, n) returns the first n characters, RIGHT(text, n) the last n, and MID(text, start, n) takes n characters starting at position start. LEN(text) returns the number of characters, including spaces and hyphens. FIND(find_text, within_text) returns the position of the first match and is case sensitive; SEARCH does the same but ignores case.

Take the reference HMRC-2024-00731, which has 15 characters. =LEN(A1) returns 15. =FIND("-",A1) returns 5, the position of the first hyphen. =LEFT(A1,FIND("-",A1)-1) returns HMRC, because it takes the four characters before the hyphen. =MID(A1,6,4) returns 2024, and =RIGHT(A1,5) returns 00731.

The result of a text function is text, even if it looks like a number. =RIGHT(A1,5) gives the text "00731", with the leading zeros intact. Wrap it in VALUE to turn it into the number 731, and note that the leading zeros disappear.

TRIM removes extra spaces from the start and end and reduces runs of spaces between words to one. PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word, so PROPER("jane SMITH") gives Jane Smith. UPPER and LOWER change the case. SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new) replaces text, and the ampersand (&) joins pieces together: =A1&" "&B1.

TEXT converts a value to text with a format, such as =TEXT(0.256,"0.0%"), which gives 25.6%. Use it when you build a sentence with a number inside, for example ="Success rate: "&TEXT(B2,"0%").

questions.prompt: With HMRC-2024-00731 in A1, what does =LEFT(A1,FIND("-",A1)-1) return?

options.text: HMRC-
HMR
HMRC

questions.hint: FIND returns 5, so LEFT takes the first 4 characters.

questions.prompt: With HMRC-2024-00731 in A1, which formula returns the year 2024?

options.text: =LEFT(A1,9)

questions.hint: Position 6 is the first digit after the first hyphen, and four characters are taken.

questions.prompt: What type of result does =RIGHT(A1,5) give for HMRC-2024-00731?

options.text: The text 00731, with its leading zeros kept
The text -00731 including the hyphen
The number 731 with the zeros dropped
The number 73100

questions.hint: Text functions return text, so leading zeros survive until VALUE converts it.

questions.prompt: What does =VALUE(RIGHT(A1,5)) return, with the text 00731 as the last five characters?

options.text: #VALUE!

questions.hint: VALUE converts the text to a number, so the leading zeros drop away.

questions.prompt: What does =LEN(A1) return for HMRC-2024-00731?
questions.hint: Letters, digits and both hyphens all count: 4+1+4+1+5.

questions.prompt: Which function turns the text "jane SMITH" into "Jane Smith"?

options.text: UPPER
PROPER
LOWER
TRIM

questions.hint: PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word and lowers the rest.

questions.prompt: Cells A1 holds Jane and B1 holds Smith. Which formula returns Jane Smith with a space between?

options.text: =CONCATENATE(A1,B1)

questions.hint: The ampersand joins text, and the quoted space adds the gap.

questions.prompt: What does =TEXT(0.256,"0.0%") return?
questions.hint: The format multiplies by 100 and shows one decimal place.

questions.prompt: A name in A1 is "  Ali   Khan " with extra spaces. What does =TRIM(A1) return?

options.text: Ali  Khan
AliKhan
Ali-Khan
Ali Khan

questions.hint: TRIM removes leading and trailing spaces and reduces inner gaps to a single space.

questions.prompt: Why does the formula =FIND("hmrc",A1) return #VALUE! for HMRC-2024-00731?

options.text: FIND needs a third argument
The text is longer than FIND allows
FIND is case sensitive and finds no lower-case match
FIND only works on numbers

questions.hint: Using SEARCH instead would ignore case and find the match.

items.title: L6: Spreadsheets: dates, working days and deadlines
items.source: Microsoft Support: date and time functions, NETWORKDAYS, WORKDAY, EDATE and DATEDIF
items.body:
Excel stores a date as a number: the count of days since 30 December 1899. For example, 1 January 2025 is stored as 45658. That is why you can add and subtract dates. If A1 holds 1 January 2025, =A1+30 gives 31 January 2025. If a date is typed in a form Excel does not recognise, it is stored as text, aligns left by default and cannot be used in date calculations.

Subtracting one date from another returns the number of days between them. 10 February 2025 to 25 February 2025 is 15 days. A date minus date does not count the start day itself.

WORKDAY(start, days, [holidays]) returns the date after a number of working days, skipping Saturdays and Sundays and any dates in the holidays list. Starting on Monday 3 March 2025, =WORKDAY(A1,10) returns Monday 17 March 2025. NETWORKDAYS(start, end, [holidays]) counts working days between two dates and includes both the start and end dates. From Monday 3 March to Friday 14 March 2025 it returns 10.

EDATE(date, months) moves a date by whole months. EDATE of 31 January 2025 plus 1 month is 28 February 2025, because Excel uses the last day of a shorter month. EOMONTH returns the last day of a month. DATEDIF(start, end, "Y") returns completed years, "M" completed months and "D" days.

TODAY() returns the current date and recalculates every time the file opens, so results change. Avoid it in a record that should stay fixed, and type the date as a value instead. Format dates with TEXT(A1,"dd mmmm yyyy") when they go inside a sentence.

questions.prompt: A1 holds Monday 3 March 2025. What does =WORKDAY(A1,10) return, with no holidays list?

options.text: Thursday 13 March 2025
Friday 14 March 2025
Monday 13 March 2025
Monday 17 March 2025

questions.hint: Ten working days is two full weeks, and weekends are skipped.

questions.prompt: What does =NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2025,3,3),DATE(2025,3,14)) return?
questions.hint: It counts weekdays from Monday 3 March to Friday 14 March, including both ends.

questions.prompt: What does =EDATE(DATE(2025,1,31),1) return?

options.text: 3 March 2025
1 March 2025
31 February 2025
28 February 2025

questions.hint: Excel returns the last day of the month when the target day does not exist.

questions.prompt: What number does =DATE(2025,2,25)-DATE(2025,2,10) return?
questions.hint: Subtracting dates gives the days between them, without counting the start day.

questions.prompt: A1 holds 1 January 2025. What does =A1+30 return?

options.text: 1 February 2025
30 January 2025
30 days as text
31 January 2025

questions.hint: Adding 30 to the stored day number moves the date forward 30 days.

questions.prompt: A date typed as 'third March' shows left-aligned and will not work in =A1+7. What has happened?

options.text: The column is too narrow to show the date
Excel stored it as text, not as a date
The date is outside the calendar range
The cell format is set to currency

questions.hint: Left alignment and failing calculations point to text rather than a date value.

questions.prompt: Which function should you use for a service level of 15 working days after the date a case was received?

options.text: EOMONTH
TODAY
WORKDAY
EDATE

questions.hint: WORKDAY adds a number of working days and can skip bank holidays if you supply a list.

questions.prompt: Why is TODAY() a poor choice for recording the date a case was closed?

options.text: It recalculates each time the file opens, so the recorded date keeps changing
It cannot be formatted as a date
It stores the time but not the date
It only works for dates in the future

questions.hint: A fixed date must be typed in as a value if it should never change.

questions.prompt: What does =DATEDIF(DATE(2020,1,1),DATE(2025,3,15),"Y") return?
questions.hint: There are five completed years between 1 January 2020 and 15 March 2025.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives a sentence such as 'Reply by 17 March 2025' from a date in B2?

options.text: ="Reply by "&B2
="Reply by "&TEXT(B2,"d mmmm yyyy")
="Reply by "+B2
="Reply by "&VALUE(B2)

questions.hint: Joining the date directly would show its serial number, so TEXT formats it.

items.title: L6: OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE and need to know
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy (Cabinet Office); GOV.UK guidance on working with government information
items.body:
The Government Security Classifications Policy has three classifications: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET. Most government information is OFFICIAL, and it needs sensible, everyday protection. OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE is not a fourth classification. It is a handling caveat that is added to OFFICIAL information whose loss or disclosure could have more damaging consequences. Examples are some personal data, commercial negotiations and sensitive policy advice.

A descriptor can be added to explain the sensitivity. Common ones include PERSONAL, COMMERCIAL and LOCSEN (location sensitive). The marking is normally placed at the top and bottom of documents and often in the subject line or file name of an email, so the recipient knows how to handle it.

Need to know is the principle that people should only see sensitive information if they need it to do their job. Having a security clearance, or a senior grade, does not give a right to see everything. Share sensitive material with named people rather than large groups, and check distribution lists before sending.

Typical handling for OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE: send it only through approved government systems, do not use personal email or personal cloud storage, avoid discussing it where you can be overheard, store paper copies in a locked cabinet when not in use, and take care when printing. Use an approved method to dispose of paper, such as a confidential waste bin or a shredder. If you are unsure of the classification, ask the information asset owner or your security team rather than guessing.

Aggregation can raise sensitivity: a large collection of OFFICIAL records, such as a database of citizens' details, may need more protection than any single record.

questions.prompt: What is OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE in the Government Security Classifications Policy?

options.text: A handling caveat added to OFFICIAL information that needs extra care
The classification for information that is secret but not top secret
A marking used only for information about named individuals
A fourth classification between OFFICIAL and SECRET

questions.hint: The policy has three classifications, and OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE is a caveat within OFFICIAL.

questions.prompt: Which is a common descriptor that can be used with OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE?

options.text: PUBLIC
COMMERCIAL
RESTRICTED
URGENT

questions.hint: Descriptors such as PERSONAL, COMMERCIAL and LOCSEN explain why the information is sensitive.

questions.prompt: A colleague with a high grade asks you for OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE casework that has nothing to do with their role. What is the right response?

options.text: Send it to their personal email so it is kept separate
Send it only if they promise to delete it afterwards
Check whether they need it for their job and refuse if they do not
Send it because their grade means they can see everything

questions.hint: Need to know applies whatever someone's seniority.

questions.prompt: You need to send an OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE report to three named colleagues. What is the best approach?

options.text: Upload it to a free file-sharing site and email the link
Send to the named colleagues only, using the approved government email system, with the marking included
Send it to your personal address so you can edit it at home
Send it to the whole team list so no one is missed

questions.hint: Limit distribution to those who need it and use approved systems.

questions.prompt: Where is a protective marking normally placed on a document?

options.text: Only on the first page
At the top and bottom of each page
Only in the footer of the final page
Only in the file name

questions.hint: Top and bottom markings make the classification visible on every page.

questions.prompt: You are on a train and need to read OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Read it freely since the train is not a government building
Read it on a personal tablet so it stays off your work device
Leave it at the seat for a few minutes while you buy a drink
Avoid reading it or discussing it where others can see or overhear

questions.hint: Reducing the chance of overlooking or overhearing is basic handling.

questions.prompt: A large database of customers' names and addresses is held on a shared drive. Why might the whole collection need more protection than a single record?

options.text: Because a single record has no data protection value
Aggregation of many records can increase the impact if it is lost
Because databases are always classified SECRET
Because the shared drive rules only apply to databases

questions.hint: The combined impact of losing many records may be greater than losing one.

questions.prompt: You are unsure how to classify a new document. What should you do?

options.text: Mark it SECRET to be safe
Leave it unmarked and decide later
Ask the information asset owner or security team
Copy the marking from the last document you wrote

questions.hint: Over- and under-classifying both cause harm, so seek advice.

questions.prompt: What is a suitable way to dispose of printed OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE papers?

options.text: Fold them in half and put them in the recycling bin
Put them in a confidential waste bin or shred them
Tear them once and leave them in the open bin
Take them home and put them in your household recycling

questions.hint: Approved disposal prevents others from reading discarded information.

items.title: L6: Subject access requests: the process
items.source: UK GDPR Articles 12 and 15; ICO guidance: Right of access
items.body:
Under the UK GDPR, people have the right to access their personal data, known as a subject access request or SAR. The person is entitled to a copy of their personal data and some supplementary information, such as why you hold it, who it is shared with and how long it will be kept.

A request does not have to be in writing or use any special words. It can be made by letter, email, telephone, through social media or to any member of staff, and it is still valid. Pass it to the right team immediately, because the clock has started.

The time limit is one calendar month starting from the day you receive the request, or from the day you receive any information you need to confirm identity or clarify a request, if you have properly asked for it. If the date in the following month does not exist, the deadline is the last day of that month. For example, a request received on 31 January is due by 28 February in a non-leap year. If the request is complex or the person has made several requests, you can extend by up to two further months, but you must tell the person within the first month and explain why.

There is normally no fee. You may charge a reasonable fee or refuse only if a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive. Check the identity of the requester using reasonable means, without asking for more than you need.

If the information includes another person's data, you must decide whether it is reasonable to disclose it, or whether you can redact it. You have a right to withhold some information, for example where an exemption applies. Explain what you have withheld and why where you can.

questions.prompt: A customer phones a front-line adviser and says they want a copy of everything the department holds about them. What is the position?

options.text: It is not valid until the customer puts it in writing
It is valid only once the customer pays the fee
It is valid only if the customer uses the words 'subject access request'
It is a valid SAR and the adviser should pass it on straight away

questions.hint: A SAR can be made verbally to any member of staff and the time limit starts on receipt.

questions.prompt: A SAR is received on 15 January 2025 and is not complex. When is the response due?

options.text: 31 January 2025
15 February 2025
15 March 2025
28 February 2025

questions.hint: The deadline is one calendar month from receipt: the same date in the next month.

questions.prompt: A SAR is received on 31 January 2025, which is not a leap year. When is the response due?

options.text: 3 March 2025
1 March 2025
28 February 2025
31 February 2025

questions.hint: If the corresponding date does not exist, the deadline is the last day of that month.

questions.prompt: When can the time limit be extended by up to two further months?

options.text: When the request is complex or the person has made a number of requests, and you tell them within the first month
Whenever the team is short of staff
When the request arrives during a busy period for the department
When the person has not yet paid the fee

questions.hint: Extensions are for complexity or multiple requests and must be communicated in time.

questions.prompt: What is the normal rule about charging a fee for a SAR?

options.text: A flat fee of £10 is always required
Normally no fee is charged
A fee can be charged if the file is more than 50 pages
A fee is required if the request is made by email

questions.hint: A fee may be charged only for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests.

questions.prompt: The department is not sure who the requester is. What should it do?

options.text: Refuse the request unless a passport is provided
Send the data and ask for identity afterwards
Ask for reasonable proof of identity, only what is needed
Ask for three forms of ID in every case

questions.hint: Check identity proportionately, without asking for more than necessary.

questions.prompt: A file requested in a SAR includes comments from a named neighbour who made a complaint. What should you do?

options.text: Always send the file unredacted because the requester is the subject
Ask the neighbour to approve every request
Consider whether it is reasonable to disclose the neighbour's data, and redact where it is not
Refuse the entire request because it contains third-party data

questions.hint: Third-party data requires a balance, but it does not justify blanket refusal.

questions.prompt: Which information must a SAR response include beyond the copy of the data?

options.text: The purposes of processing, who it is shared with, and how long it is kept
A copy of the department's whole data protection policy
A list of all staff who have accessed the file
The personal data of other people in the same case

questions.hint: The right of access also covers supplementary information about the processing.

questions.prompt: When may a department refuse a SAR or charge a reasonable fee?

options.text: When it is manifestly unfounded or excessive
When the requester is currently in dispute with the department
When the requester has made a request before
When responding would take more than a day

questions.hint: Only these narrow circumstances permit a refusal or fee.

items.title: L6: Taking minutes and action notes
items.source: Cabinet Office guidance on records management; National Archives guidance on creating records
items.body:
Minutes are a short, accurate record of what a meeting decided and who will do what. They are not a word-for-word account. A good set of minutes records the date, time and place, who attended and who sent apologies, the decisions that were reached, the actions agreed and any key points of the discussion that explain why a decision was made.

Prepare before the meeting. Read the agenda and papers, set up a template with the agenda items as headings, and ask the chair how much detail they want. During the meeting, note decisions and actions as they are agreed and ask the chair to clarify if you are unsure. Do not record every comment or attribute opinions to individuals unless asked to, but be accurate if the point matters.

Each action should have a clear owner and a due date, for example 'Sam to send the draft to the legal team by 14 March'. An action with no owner or date is easily forgotten. Many teams record actions in a separate action log that is updated after each meeting.

Write the minutes soon after the meeting, while it is fresh, and send a draft to the chair to check before it goes to everyone. Use the past tense for the discussion and plain language. Mark any sensitive content appropriately and think about who should receive the minutes.

At the next meeting, minutes are normally agreed as an accurate record in the 'minutes of the last meeting' item, and then 'matters arising' deals with the actions. Once agreed, they are kept as a record.

Minutes can be disclosed under the Freedom of Information Act, so write them in a way that would stand up if released.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of minutes?

options.text: To show how long each item took
To record each person's opinions so that they can be quoted later
To provide a word-for-word transcript of everything said
To record the decisions made and the actions agreed

questions.hint: Minutes are a summary of outcomes, not a transcript.

questions.prompt: Which action note is written best?

options.text: Legal team to be sent the draft.
Draft to be sent soon.
Everyone to consider the draft before the next meeting.
Sam to send the draft to the legal team by 14 March.

questions.hint: A good action has a named owner and a due date.

questions.prompt: The chair has just said 'Let's go with option B'. What should the minute-taker do?

options.text: Wait until the end of the meeting and ask for the decisions
Record the decision and, if unclear, check with the chair that it has been agreed
Record only the discussion that led to option B
Leave it out of the minutes as it was not formally voted on

questions.hint: Decisions are the most important thing to capture and confirm.

questions.prompt: When should draft minutes be written and checked?

options.text: Soon after the meeting, and the chair should check the draft before it is circulated
Before the meeting, using the agenda to predict what will be said
Within a month, once all attendees have emailed their comments
After the next meeting, when the actions are complete

questions.hint: Writing quickly helps accuracy, and the chair confirms that it is an accurate record.

questions.prompt: What happens to minutes at the start of the next meeting?

options.text: They are sent to the Information Commissioner
They are rewritten to take account of what was decided afterwards
They are checked and agreed as an accurate record
They are destroyed once the actions are done

questions.hint: Agreement as a true record makes the minutes authoritative.

questions.prompt: In a meeting, someone makes a joking personal comment about a customer. How should you handle it in the minutes?

options.text: Record who said it so they can be held to account
Record it word for word so it is accurate
Summarise it as an action for the chair
Leave it out, as it is not relevant to a decision or action

questions.hint: Minutes record outcomes and relevant reasoning, not every remark.

questions.prompt: Why might minutes need to be written carefully with disclosure in mind?

options.text: They can be requested under the Freedom of Information Act
They are always published on GOV.UK
They are reviewed by the Auditor General every year
They are exempt from disclosure once agreed

questions.hint: Minutes are held information, so write them to stand up if released.

questions.prompt: What is the term for the agenda item where actions from earlier meetings are reviewed?

options.text: Any other business
Matters arising
Apologies for absence
Declarations of interest

questions.hint: Matters arising covers progress on earlier actions and points left over from past minutes.

questions.prompt: An attendee asks you to change the minutes to show they raised an objection that they did not make. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the item from the minutes entirely
Add the objection but mark it as a late addition
Add the objection so as to keep the peace
Decline and explain that minutes must be an accurate record, and refer it to the chair if needed

questions.hint: Accuracy matters; changing the record to suit someone undermines integrity.

items.title: L6: Basic analysis: averages, change and charts
items.source: Government Analysis Function: guidance on presenting data and charts; Office for National Statistics
items.body:
Choose the right average. The mean adds all the values and divides by the number of values. The median is the middle value when they are in order, or the mean of the two middle values if there is an even number. The median is less affected by extreme values. If five days produced 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14 cases, the mean is 7 and the median is 5. Add a sixth day with 60 cases and the mean rises to 15.8 (rounded), but the median is 6.5. A single outlier has changed the mean a lot and the median only a little. The mode is the most common value, here 5.

Percentage change is (new minus old) divided by old, times 100. A rise from 60 to 72 is a 20 per cent increase. A fall from 72 to 60 is a 16.7 per cent decrease, not 20 per cent, because the base is different. A percentage point change is the simple difference between two percentages. A rate rising from 82% to 88% is a 6 percentage point rise, which is about a 7.3 per cent increase on the original rate.

A rate shows how often something happens relative to a population: 450 cases among 18,000 people is 25 per 1,000. Rates allow fair comparison between groups of different sizes.

For charts, use a line chart to show change over time, a bar chart to compare categories and a pie chart only for a few parts of a whole. Start a bar chart's axis at zero, because a truncated axis exaggerates differences. Label axes, include units, give a clear title that states the message and cite the source. Avoid 3D effects and decoration.

Correlation does not prove cause: two things moving together may both be influenced by a third factor.

questions.prompt: Five days produced 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14 cases. What is the median?
questions.hint: With an odd number of values the median is the middle one when sorted.

questions.prompt: A sixth day of 60 cases is added to 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14. What is the new median?
questions.hint: With six values, the median is the mean of the third and fourth: 5 and 8.

questions.prompt: Why does the median change less than the mean when one very large value is added?

options.text: The median ignores the new value completely
The median depends on position in the ordered list, not on how large the extreme value is
The median is always the smallest value
The mean cannot be calculated with large numbers

questions.hint: An outlier pulls the mean upward, but the median only shifts by position.

questions.prompt: Cases rise from 60 to 72. What is the percentage increase?
questions.hint: The change of 12 is divided by the starting value of 60.

questions.prompt: Cases fall from 72 back to 60. What is the percentage decrease?
questions.hint: The change of 12 is divided by the new starting value of 72.

questions.prompt: A pass rate rises from 82% to 88%. How should the change be described most precisely?

options.text: A rise of 6 per cent
A rise of 7.3 percentage points
A rise of 82 per cent
A rise of 6 percentage points

questions.hint: The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points.

questions.prompt: 450 cases occurred among 18,000 people. What is the rate per 1,000 people?
questions.hint: 450 divided by 18,000, multiplied by 1,000.

questions.prompt: Which chart is usually best for showing monthly case numbers over two years?

options.text: A 3D column chart with a different colour for each month
A line chart
A pie chart
A table of percentages without a chart

questions.hint: Line charts show trends and change over time most clearly.

questions.prompt: Why should a bar chart's value axis normally start at zero?

options.text: Bar charts cannot display numbers over 100
Software always starts bar charts at zero
Zero makes the bars wider and easier to see
